source_refs.note: Practice long questions written from Chapter 17 (PDF 85-117, printed 81-113); not printed in the book. Based on the chapter's text, tables, boxes and worked examples (numericals with changed values); none repeats the chapter exercise. Drafts needing academic review.

blocks.text: Practice long questions for the whole of Chapter 17 (Alternating Current), in the shape of a Board long question: each theory question of 5 marks (define, explain, derive) is followed by a numerical of 3 marks on the same topic. Each question has a model answer; the numericals are solved step by step.

blocks.prompt: 1 What is alternating current? State the conditions for a voltage to be alternating. Define the peak, peak-to-peak, average and rms values of an alternating voltage and write their relations with the peak value. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Alternating current: a sinusoidally varying current represented by time dependent sine or cosine functions. The emf of an AC generator is
V = Vₒ sin ωt ... (17.1), and similarly I = Iₒ sin ωt
where Vₒ is the maximum voltage and ω the angular frequency.

Conditions: (i) every cycle (one time period T) has two exactly symmetrical half-cycles, one positive and one negative, so the direction of current (polarity of voltage) reverses after every half-cycle; (ii) the peak value on both sides remains constant in all cycles. The quantity changes most rapidly at the zero crossover points and most slowly at its peaks.

Instantaneous value: V = Vₒ sin ωt; as ω = 2π/T and f = 1/T, V = Vₒ sin (2πft).

Peak value (Vₒ, Iₒ): the highest value reached in one cycle.
Peak-to-peak value: the distance from the positive to the negative peak; Vp-p = 2Vₒ.
Average value: the full-cycle average is zero because the two halves cancel, so it is taken over one half-cycle (0 to π). For a full-wave rectified sine wave Iₐᵥ = 0.637 Iₒ and Vₐᵥ = 0.637 Vₒ.
rms value: the value of a constant current (voltage) that produces the same power in a resistor as the alternating current (voltage):
Iᵣₘₛ = Iₒ/√2 = 0.707 Iₒ ... (17.3)
Vᵣₘₛ = Vₒ/√2 = 0.707 Vₒ ... (17.4)

book_ref.quote: The emf of an AC generator is given by the following equation, for voltage:

blocks.prompt: 2 A 50 Hz supply has an rms voltage of 230 V. Find (i) its peak value (ii) its peak-to-peak value (iii) the half-cycle average value (iv) the instantaneous voltage at t = 1/600 s, taking V = 0 at t = 0. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Go from rms to peak with Vₒ = Vᵣₘₛ/0.707, then use 2Vₒ, 0.637 Vₒ and V = Vₒ sin (2πft).

book_ref.quote: rms values represent the direct current, or voltage, values that will produce the same heating effect

blocks.prompt: 3 Define instantaneous power and mean power in an AC circuit. Show that for a sinusoidal current in a resistive load the mean power is half the maximum power, and explain the reason physically. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
A resistive load does not store energy (as a capacitor or inductor does); it simply dissipates energy as heat.

Instantaneous power: the power at any moment t,
P = VI ... (17.5)
where V and I are the instantaneous voltage and current. The maximum power occurs when V and I are at their peaks Vₒ and Iₒ.
Mean power: the average power over one complete cycle of the AC waveform.

Relation: For a sinusoidal AC with peak current Iₒ through resistance R,
Pₘₐₓ = Iₒ²R ... (17.6)
Pₘₑₐₙ = Iᵣₘₛ²R ... (17.7)
As Iₒ = √2 Iᵣₘₛ, Eq. 17.6 becomes
Pₘₐₓ = (√2 Iᵣₘₛ)²R = 2Iᵣₘₛ²R
From Eq. 17.7, Iᵣₘₛ²R = Pₘₑₐₙ, thus
Pₘₐₓ = 2Pₘₑₐₙ, or Pₘₑₐₙ = Pₘₐₓ/2 ... (17.8)

Reason: the instantaneous power varies over the cycle. It reaches its maximum value only at certain points and spends significant time at zero or lower values, so its average is half the peak value.

book_ref.quote: Therefore, it can be concluded that the mean power in a resistive load is half the maximum power

blocks.prompt: 4 A sinusoidal current of peak value 4 A flows through a 60 Ω resistor. Find (i) the maximum power (ii) the mean power (iii) the rms current, and check that Iᵣₘₛ²R gives the same mean power. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Use Pₘₐₓ = Iₒ²R, then halve it; find Iᵣₘₛ = 0.707 Iₒ and use Pₘₑₐₙ = Iᵣₘₛ²R as a check.

book_ref.quote: The maximum or peak Pₘₐₓ occurs when the current and voltage are at their peak values

blocks.final_answer: Pₘₐₓ = 960 W; Pₘₑₐₙ = 480 W; Iᵣₘₛ = 2.83 A (Iᵣₘₛ²R ≈ 480 W, as expected)

blocks.prompt: 5 Discuss the flow of AC through a pure resistor. Show that the voltage and current are in phase, draw (in words) its vector diagram, and obtain the expressions for instantaneous and average power. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Let a resistor R be connected with an AC source. The instantaneous voltage is
V = Vₒ sin ωt ... (17.10)
The instantaneous current is I = V/R. Using Eq. 17.10,
I = (Vₒ sin ωt)/R
I = Iₒ sin ωt ... (17.11)
where Iₒ = Vₒ/R is the peak current.

Phase: Eqs. 17.10 and 17.11 are sine functions of the same ωt, so V and I pass their maximum and minimum values at the same time: they are in phase.
Vector diagram: V_R and I_R are drawn parallel, because there is no phase difference between them. The opposition is the resistance R = V/I.

Power: the power dissipation is proportional to I², so it does not matter whether the current is direct or alternating. But an AC of peak Iₒ is at that value only for an instant in each half-cycle, so it gives less heating than a DC of value Iₒ. Instantaneous power:
P = VI or P = I²R or P = V²/R ... (17.12)
Average power: ⟨P⟩ = ⟨I²R⟩. As ⟨I²⟩ = Iₒ²/2 = Iᵣₘₛ²,
⟨P⟩ = (Iₒ²/2)R = Iᵣₘₛ²R, and also ⟨P⟩ = IᵣₘₛVᵣₘₛ
P is in watts, V in volts, I in amperes and R in ohms; Eq. 17.12 holds only when V and I are in phase.

book_ref.quote: A resistor R connected with an AC source is shown in Fig.17.6 (a).

blocks.prompt: 6 A 1.5 kW heating element works on a 230 V rms AC supply. Find (i) the rms current taken (ii) the resistance of the element when hot (iii) the peak current. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: For a resistor V and I are in phase, so P = VI with rms values; then R = V/I and Iₒ = Iᵣₘₛ/0.707.

book_ref.quote: Calculate the amount of current taken from the supply and the resistance of the element when it is hot.

blocks.prompt: 7 An AC source of frequency f is connected to a pure inductor L. Show that the voltage across the inductor leads the current by π/2, obtain the expression for its reactance, and explain why an inductor allows DC but opposes AC. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
An inductor (coil or choke) is a passive two-terminal component with large self-inductance and negligible resistance that stores energy in a magnetic field.

Let the current be I = Iₒ sin ωt ... (17.13)
The changing current sets up a back emf of magnitude V = L ΔI/Δt. The applied voltage must equal this back emf:
V = L (Δ/Δt)(Iₒ sin ωt) = LIₒ (Δ/Δt) sin ωt ... (17.14)
As (Δ/Δt) sin ωt = ω cos ωt,
V = ωLIₒ cos ωt
As ωLIₒ = Vₒ, V = Vₒ cos ωt
As cos ωt = sin (ωt + π/2),
V = Vₒ sin (ωt + π/2) ... (17.15)
So the voltage across L leads the current by 90° (π/2 rad); the current always lags behind the voltage by 90°.

Inductive reactance: X_L = Vᵣₘₛ/Iᵣₘₛ ... (17.16)
As Vᵣₘₛ = 0.707 Vₒ and Iᵣₘₛ = 0.707 Iₒ, X_L = Vₒ/Iₒ
As Vₒ = ωLIₒ, X_L = ωLIₒ/Iₒ
X_L = ωL = 2πfL ... (17.17)
Its unit is ohm. X_L is directly proportional to both f and L.

DC and AC: for DC, f = 0, so X_L = 0 and the inductor allows DC. For AC of large frequency X_L is large, so the inductor blocks (opposes) AC. Since the phase difference is 90°, a pure inductor dissipates no average power; it is used to control AC without consuming energy.

book_ref.quote: Suppose an inductor of inductance L is connected with an AC source of frequency f

blocks.prompt: 8 A coil of inductance 0.5 H and negligible resistance is connected to a 220 V, 50 Hz supply. Find (i) its reactance (ii) the rms current. (iii) What would the current be if the frequency were 100 Hz? (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: X_L = 2πfL, then I = V/X_L; X_L doubles when f doubles, so the current halves.

book_ref.quote: while in case of large AC frequency, X_L is also large

blocks.final_answer: X_L = 157.1 Ω; Iᵣₘₛ = 1.40 A at 50 Hz and 0.700 A at 100 Hz

blocks.prompt: 9 What is a choke? Explain why a choke coil dissipates practically no power, and describe its uses in circuits. (5 marks)

book_ref.quote: A choke is often modeled as a series RL-circuit

blocks.prompt: 10 A choke of inductance 0.8 H and resistance 2 Ω is connected to a 220 V, 50 Hz supply. Find (i) its reactance (ii) the phase angle and power factor (iii) the current and the power dissipated. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Treat the choke as series RL: X_L = 2πfL, θ = tan⁻¹(ωL/R), Z = √(R² + X_L²), I = V/Z and P = I²R.

book_ref.quote: As the resistance R of a choke coil is negligibly small

blocks.final_answer: X_L = 251.3 Ω; θ = 89.5°, power factor ≈ 0.008; I = 0.875 A; only 1.53 W is dissipated

blocks.prompt: 11 Explain how alternating current flows through a circuit containing a capacitor. Prove that the current leads the applied voltage by a quarter of a cycle, and derive the capacitive reactance. How does it vary with frequency? (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
A capacitor does not pass DC because of the insulating medium between its plates. When an alternating voltage is applied, the capacitor is charged in one direction and then in the other as the voltage reverses; electrons move to and fro around the circuit, which constitutes alternating current.

Let V = Vₒ sin ωt ... (17.18)
q = CV holds at every instant, so the charge is q = CVₒ sin ωt.
I = Δq/Δt = (Δ/Δt)(CVₒ sin ωt) = CVₒ (Δ/Δt)(sin ωt)
As (Δ/Δt) sin ωt = ω cos ωt,
I = ωCVₒ cos ωt
As cos ωt = sin (ωt + π/2),
I = ωCVₒ sin (ωt + π/2)
Here ωCVₒ = Iₒ, thus
I = Iₒ sin (ωt + π/2) ... (17.19)
Comparing Eqs. 17.18 and 17.19, the capacitor current leads the voltage by 90° (π/2 rad, a quarter cycle), i.e. the voltage lags behind the current.

Capacitive reactance: X_C = Vᵣₘₛ/Iᵣₘₛ
As Vᵣₘₛ = 0.707 Vₒ and Iᵣₘₛ = 0.707 Iₒ, X_C = Vₒ/Iₒ
As Iₒ = ωCVₒ,
X_C = 1/ωC = 1/(2πfC), where ω = 2πf. Unit: ohm.

Frequency: at low frequency X_C is large and the current is small; at high frequency X_C is small and the current through the same capacitor is large. For DC, f = 0 and X_C = ∞, so the capacitor blocks DC.

book_ref.quote: The basic relationship between charge q and the voltage V across the plates

blocks.prompt: 12 A 4 μF capacitor is connected to a 220 V rms supply. Find its reactance and the rms current (i) at 50 Hz (ii) at 500 Hz. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: X_C = 1/(2πfC), then I = V/X_C; ten times the frequency gives one tenth the reactance and ten times the current.

book_ref.quote: Which shows that for low frequencies, capacitor will have a large reactance

blocks.prompt: 13 Define impedance. A resistor R and a capacitor C are connected in series to an AC source. Using the voltage phasors, derive the impedance of the circuit and the phase angle between voltage and current, and write the power consumed. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Impedance: the combined effect of resistance and reactances in an AC circuit; Z = Vᵣₘₛ/Iᵣₘₛ ... (17.20), SI unit ohm.

RC series: as R and C are in series, the same current flows through both; take the current as reference.
Voltage across R: V_R = IᵣₘₛR, in phase with the current (drawn along the current line).
Voltage across C: V_C = IᵣₘₛX_C = Iᵣₘₛ/ωC, lagging behind the current by 90° (drawn at right angles to the current line).
The applied voltage is the vector resultant:
Vᵣₘₛ = √(V_R² + V_C²)
Vᵣₘₛ = √((IᵣₘₛR)² + (Iᵣₘₛ/ωC)²)
Vᵣₘₛ = Iᵣₘₛ√(R² + (1/ωC)²)
Impedance Z = Vᵣₘₛ/Iᵣₘₛ = √(R² + (1/ωC)²) ... (17.21)

Impedance diagram: R is a horizontal line along the current; X_C = 1/ωC is drawn lagging the R line by 90°; Z is their vector sum. The angle θ of Z with the R line is the phase difference; the current leads the applied voltage by
θ = tan⁻¹(X_C/R) = tan⁻¹(1/ωCR) = tan⁻¹(1/2πfCR)

Power: the capacitor only stores energy and does not dissipate it, so the power is consumed by the resistor:
P = I²R, or P = VI cos θ ... (17.22)

book_ref.quote: Consider a network of resistance R and a capacitor C connected in series

blocks.prompt: 14 A 300 Ω resistor and a 10 μF capacitor are connected in series across a 220 V, 50 Hz supply. Find (i) the capacitive reactance (ii) the impedance and current (iii) the phase angle (iv) the power consumed. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Find X_C, add it to R as vectors to get Z, then I = V/Z, θ = tan⁻¹(X_C/R) and P = I²R.

book_ref.quote: A resistor of resistance 5 kΩ is connected in series with capacitor

blocks.final_answer: X_C = 318.3 Ω; Z = 437.4 Ω; I = 0.503 A; θ = 46.7° with current leading; P = 75.9 W

blocks.prompt: 15 A resistor R and an inductor L are connected in series with an AC source. Derive the impedance of the circuit and the phase angle between the applied voltage and current. What is power factor, and where is the power consumed? (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
As R and L are in series, the same current flows through both.
Voltage across R: V_R = IᵣₘₛR, in phase with the current (line OA).
Voltage across L: V_L = IᵣₘₛX_L, ahead of the current by 90° (line OB).
The resultant voltage is their vector sum (line OP):
Vᵣₘₛ = √(V_R² + V_L²)
Vᵣₘₛ = √((IᵣₘₛR)² + (IᵣₘₛX_L)²) = Iᵣₘₛ√(R² + X_L²)
As X_L = ωL, Vᵣₘₛ = Iᵣₘₛ√(R² + (ωL)²)
Impedance Z = Vᵣₘₛ/Iᵣₘₛ = √(R² + (ωL)²) ... (17.23)
Phase angle: the angle θ which Z makes with the R line is the phase difference; the voltage leads the current by
θ = tan⁻¹(ωL/R)

Power: the inductor stores energy but ideally does not dissipate it, so the power is consumed by the resistor:
P = I²R = VI cos θ
The factor cos θ is the power factor. When DC power (e.g. from a solar panel) is converted into AC power, the inverter efficiency (usually 85% to 90%) is included: P_ac = (inverter efficiency) × P_dc.

book_ref.quote: The resultant voltage V will be the vector sum of V_R and V_L shown vectorially by line OP

blocks.prompt: 16 A 40 Ω resistor and a 0.1 H inductor are connected in series across a 220 V, 50 Hz supply. Find (i) the impedance (ii) the current (iii) the phase angle and power factor (iv) the power consumed. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Find X_L = 2πfL, then Z, I = V/Z, θ = tan⁻¹(X_L/R); the power is I²R, which equals VI cos θ.

book_ref.quote: where I, R and V represents current, resistance, and voltage respectively

blocks.final_answer: Z = 50.9 Ω; I = 4.33 A; θ = 38.1° (voltage leading), power factor 0.786; P = 748 W

blocks.prompt: 17 Write the impedance of an RLC-series circuit and explain its behaviour at high and low frequencies. Derive the resonance frequency, and state the properties of the circuit at resonance. (5 marks)

book_ref.quote: Consider a RLC-series circuit having an alternating voltage source with variable frequency

blocks.prompt: 18 An RLC-series circuit has R = 20 Ω, L = 0.2 H and C = 50 μF and is connected to a 100 V rms source of variable frequency. Find (i) the resonance frequency (ii) the current at resonance (iii) the impedance and current at 100 Hz. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Use fᵣ = 1/(2π√LC); at resonance Z = R; off resonance find X_L and X_C and use Z = √(R² + (X_L − X_C)²).

book_ref.quote: The impedance diagram of RLC-series circuit is shown in Fig.17.11(b)

steps: (ii) At resonance Z = R = 20 Ω; I = 100 V/20 Ω = 5 A
blocks.final_answer: fᵣ = 50.3 Hz; I = 5 A at resonance; at 100 Hz Z = 95.9 Ω and I = 1.04 A (the circuit is inductive there)

blocks.prompt: 19 Write the impedance of an RLC-parallel circuit. Compare the behaviour of RLC-series and RLC-parallel circuits at resonance, and explain admittance, current magnification and the quality factor of the parallel circuit. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
In an RLC-parallel circuit R, L and C are connected in parallel with the AC source; the voltage is the same across all components, so it is taken as the reference phasor. The impedance is
Z = 1/√((1/R)² + (1/X_L − 1/X_C)²) ... (17.28)
It resonates at X_L = X_C, where the second term vanishes and Z = R is maximum; the circuit behaves as purely resistive. The resonance frequency is fᵣ = 1/(2π√LC), and at resonance the power factor is unity.

Admittance: Y is the reciprocal of impedance; the total admittance of a parallel RLC circuit is the sum of the admittances of the components.
Current magnification: at resonance the source current is minimum, but the branch currents I_L and I_C may each be larger than the resonance current Iᵣ.
Quality factor: Q measures the sharpness of the resonance peak (energy stored compared with energy dissipated); for the parallel circuit Q = R√(C/L), so Q rises with R.
Uses: tuning circuits, signal processing, power systems and induction cooktops.

Comparison at resonance (table).

book_ref.quote: The impedance, admittance, and currents in a parallel RLC-circuit are all frequency-dependent.

rows: Same current through R, L and C.
Same voltage across R, L and C.
Voltage amplification across L and C.
Current magnification in the L and C branches.

blocks.prompt: 20 An RLC-parallel circuit has R = 100 Ω. Find its impedance (i) at resonance, where X_L = X_C (ii) at a frequency where X_L = 40 Ω and X_C = 60 Ω. Which is larger? (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Use Z = 1/√((1/R)² + (1/X_L − 1/X_C)²); at resonance the bracket with X_L and X_C is zero.

book_ref.quote: The resonance frequency of RLC-parallel circuit is:

steps: 100 Ω > 76.8 Ω, so the impedance is maximum at resonance
blocks.final_answer: Z = 100 Ω at resonance and 76.8 Ω off resonance: the parallel circuit's impedance is maximum at resonance

blocks.prompt: 21 What is rectification? Describe the working of a half-wave rectifier with its input and output waveforms. Explain how a smoothing capacitor reduces the ripple in a rectifier output and write the expression for the ripple voltage. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Rectification: the process of converting alternating current into direct current. A diode allows a large current when forward biased and practically zero current when reverse biased, so it can be used for rectification. It is of two types: half-wave and full-wave.

Half-wave rectifier: an alternating input voltage of period T is applied to a diode D in series with a load resistance R_L.
(i) 0 → T/2 (positive half-cycle): D is forward biased, offers very low resistance, and current flows through R_L; the potential drop across R_L follows the input.
(ii) T/2 → T (negative half-cycle): D is reverse biased, offers very high resistance, practically no current flows and the drop across R_L is almost zero.
The same repeats every cycle. The current through R_L is in one direction (DC) but flows in pulses. Input: a full sine wave; output: only the positive half-cycles, zero in between. The voltage across R_L is the output voltage.

Smoothing: rectified output is pulsating DC, unsuitable for most devices. In a capacitor filter, a capacitor is connected in parallel with the load. It charges when the rectified voltage increases and discharges when it decreases, smoothing the output and raising the average DC level. For a full-wave bridge rectifier the ripple voltage is
V_ripple = I_DC/(f_ripple C) = I_DC/(2fC), with f_ripple = 2f
where I_DC is the load current, f the input frequency and C the capacitance. A larger C gives a smaller ripple.

book_ref.quote: The working of half-wave rectifier is based on the fact that the diode allows the current flow only in one direction.

blocks.prompt: 22 A full-wave bridge rectifier works on a 50 Hz supply and gives a load current of 0.2 A. Find (i) the ripple frequency (ii) the ripple voltage with a 470 μF smoothing capacitor (iii) the ripple voltage if the capacitor is 940 μF. (iv) Without smoothing, what is the average output if the peak output is 12 V? (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Ripple frequency is 2f; V_ripple = I_DC/(2fC); the average of a full-wave rectified sine is 0.637 Vₒ.

book_ref.quote: The maximum ripple voltage present in a full-wave rectifier bridge circuit

blocks.final_answer: f_ripple = 100 Hz; V_ripple = 4.26 V with 470 μF and 2.13 V with 940 μF (doubling C halves the ripple); Vₐᵥ = 7.64 V

blocks.prompt: 23 What is self-induction? Show that the self-induced emf is ε_L = −L ΔI/Δt and that L = N Δφ/ΔI. On what factors does self-inductance depend? Define the henry. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Consider a coil in series with a battery, a switch and a rheostat. If the rheostat is moved quickly, the current through the coil changes, the magnetic flux through the coil changes, and an emf is induced in the coil itself.
Self-induction: the phenomenon in which a changing current induces an emf in the coil itself.

Let φ be the flux through one loop; the flux through N turns is Nφ. As φ is proportional to the field, which is proportional to I,
Nφ ∝ I, so Nφ = LI ... (17.29)
where L is the self-inductance of the coil.
By Faraday's law,
ε_L = −N Δφ/Δt ... (17.30)
ε_L = −Δ(Nφ)/Δt
Using Eq. 17.29, ε_L = −Δ(LI)/Δt
ε_L = −L ΔI/Δt ... (17.31)
or L = −ε_L/(ΔI/Δt) ... (17.32)
The minus sign shows that the induced emf opposes the applied voltage.
Equating Eqs. 17.30 and 17.31: −N Δφ/Δt = −L ΔI/Δt, so
L = N Δφ/ΔI ... (17.33)

Factors: (i) number of turns, (ii) area of cross-section, (iii) core material; a ferromagnetic iron core increases the flux and the inductance greatly compared with an air core.

Henry: a coil has a self-inductance of 1 H if an emf of 1 V is induced in it when the current changes at 1 A s⁻¹. Unit V s A⁻¹; dimensions [ML²T⁻²A⁻²].

book_ref.quote: If we move the rheostat quickly, the primary current through the coil will change.

blocks.prompt: 24 The current in a coil of 500 turns and self-inductance 0.3 H rises steadily from 2 A to 6 A in 0.05 s. Find (i) the rate of change of current (ii) the magnitude of the self-induced emf (iii) the change of flux through each turn. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Find ΔI/Δt, then |ε_L| = L ΔI/Δt; from L = N Δφ/ΔI, Δφ = L ΔI/N.

book_ref.quote: The self-inductance of the coil can also be defined as ratio of the emf to the rate of change of current

steps: (ii) |ε_L| = L ΔI/Δt = 0.3 H × 80 A s⁻¹ = 24 V
blocks.final_answer: ΔI/Δt = 80 A s⁻¹; |ε_L| = 24 V (opposing the rise); Δφ = 2.4 × 10⁻³ Wb per turn

blocks.prompt: 25 Show that the energy stored in an inductor carrying current I is ½LI². Hence show that the energy stored per unit volume in the magnetic field of a solenoid is B²/2μₒ. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Consider a coil connected to a battery and a switch in series. When the switch is ON, the current rises from zero to its maximum value I. The changing current induces an emf opposite to the battery, and the battery does work to move charges against it.

Work to move charge Δq: W = Δq ε_L ... (17.34)
with ε_L = L ΔI/Δt. So
W = Δq L ΔI/Δt = (Δq/Δt) L ΔI ... (17.35)
Δq/Δt is the average current while the current rises from 0 to I: Δq/Δt = (0 + I)/2 = ½I, and ΔI = I − 0 = I.
Putting the values in Eq. 17.35,
W = (½I)LI = ½LI² ... (17.36)
This work is stored as potential energy in the inductor:
U_m = ½LI² ... (17.37)
It is stored in the magnetic field and can never be negative, being proportional to I².

Energy density: for a solenoid with n turns per unit length, cross-section A and length l,
B = μₒnI, so I = B/μₒn, and L = μₒn²Al
U_m = ½ μₒn²Al (B/μₒn)²
U_m = (B²/2μₒ)(Al)
As Al = volume, U_m/volume = B²/(2μₒ)
Energy density = B²/(2μₒ) ... (17.38)

book_ref.quote: When the switch is turned ON, voltage is applied across the ends of coil

blocks.prompt: 26 A solenoid of inductance 0.06 H carries a current of 5 A, and the field inside it is 0.2 T. Taking μₒ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹, find (i) the energy stored (ii) the energy density inside it. (iii) What does the energy become if the current is doubled? (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: U_m = ½LI² and energy density = B²/(2μₒ); since U_m ∝ I², doubling I makes it four times.

book_ref.quote: This work is stored as potential energy in the inductor.

steps: (ii) Energy density = B²/(2μₒ) = (0.2 T)²/(2 × 4π × 10⁻⁷) = 1.59 × 10⁴ J m⁻³
blocks.final_answer: U_m = 0.75 J; energy density = 1.59 × 10⁴ J m⁻³; with 10 A the energy is 3.0 J

blocks.prompt: 27 What is mutual induction? Derive the expression εₛ = −M ΔIₚ/Δt for the emf induced in the secondary coil. Define mutual inductance and the henry, and list the factors on which mutual inductance depends. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Consider two coils close to each other. The primary coil is connected with a battery through a switch S and a rheostat; the secondary is connected to a galvanometer. If the primary current is changed with the rheostat, the magnetic flux around changes; this changing flux also links the secondary and induces an emf in it.
Mutual induction: the phenomenon in which a changing current in one coil induces an emf in another coil.

By Faraday's law,
εₛ = −Nₛ Δφₛ/Δt ... (17.39)
where Nₛ is the number of turns of the secondary. The net flux through the secondary, Nₛφₛ, is proportional to the field of the primary, which is proportional to Iₚ:
Nₛφₛ ∝ Iₚ, so Nₛφₛ = MIₚ ... (17.40)
where M (= Nₛφₛ/Iₚ) is the mutual inductance. Using Eq. 17.40 in Eq. 17.39,
εₛ = −Δ(Nₛφₛ)/Δt = −Δ(MIₚ)/Δt
εₛ = −M ΔIₚ/Δt ... (17.41)
The emf in the secondary is proportional to the rate of change of current in the primary; the minus sign shows it opposes the change of current in the primary.

Mutual inductance: M = εₛ/(ΔIₚ/Δt) ... (17.42), the ratio of the emf induced in the secondary to the rate of change of current in the primary. Unit V s A⁻¹ = henry: one henry is the mutual inductance of two coils in which a change of 1 A s⁻¹ in the primary induces 1 V in the secondary.

Factors: number of turns of both coils; area of cross-section; permeability of the medium between them; material on which they are wound; distance between them; their orientation.
Applications: transformers, motors, generators, pacemakers and metal detectors.
